items.title: What to Say on the Car Ride Home
items.summary: Lead with 'I love watching you play,' ask one question, and leave the coaching for another day: how to make the ride home the safest part of game day.

video.note: Interior of a car after a loss: the parent says 'I love watching you play,' asks what the most fun part was, and the child, after a quiet minute, starts talking about a teammate's catch.

intro: When coaches and researchers ask athletes about their worst memories in youth sports, one answer comes up again and again: the car ride home. Not the strikeout. The ride afterward, when a well-meaning parent reviewed it.
The ride home is where your child learns whether your love changes with the score. Six words and one question are enough to get it right.
whatToDo: Lead with 'I love watching you play.' Say it first, before anything about the game, after wins and after losses. Those six words are the whole foundation.
Ask one question, and make it about them, not the result: 'What was the most fun part?' Then listen to the whole answer without adding anything.
Let them lead. If they want to talk baseball, talk baseball. If they want to talk about the snack, talk about the snack. Silence is fine too.
Separate the result from the person. 'Tough loss' is a fact. 'You guys played badly' is a verdict. Stick to facts and feelings: 'That was a close one. How are you feeling?'
Save coaching for later, if ever. If they ask 'what did I do wrong?' say 'Want to work on it tomorrow in the yard?' The car is for being a parent, not a coach.
Model sportsmanship in your comments: praise an opponent's good play, say something kind about the umpire's hard job, thank the coach by name.
Have a post-game ritual that is the same after a win or a loss: the same snack, the same song, the same question. Your child learns that your love does not change with the score.
whatToSay: What was the most fun part?
That was a close one. How are you feeling?
Want to work on it tomorrow, or just relax?
The other team's shortstop made a great play, huh?
whatToWatchFor: They start the conversation about the game themselves, which means they expect it to be safe.
They mention a mistake without spiraling: 'I missed that grounder. Oh well.'
They talk about teammates and fun moments more than about the score.
They are relaxed and chatty, not quiet and tense, when they get in the car.
whatToAvoid: Opening with the mistake: 'What happened on that pop-up?' That question will be remembered for years.
Criticizing the coach, the umpire, or teammates in front of your child. It teaches blame, and it gets repeated in the dugout.
Reviewing the game play by play. They lived it. They do not need the replay.
Comparing: 'Did you see how hard the other kids were trying?'
Making the car ride the only time you talk about sports. If every ride is a debrief, they will dread the car.
ifStruggling: If every ride turns into tears or silence, say nothing about the game for a full month. Just the six words and the snack.
Write the six words on a sticky note on the dashboard where you can see it and they cannot.
Let them put on headphones. Space is a gift after a hard game.
If you are too upset about the game yourself, say 'I'm going to be quiet for a bit,' and be quiet. Take care of your own feelings before you talk.
makeItFun: High-Low-Funny: everyone in the car shares a high, a low, and a funny thing from the day, parent included. The game becomes one of many things that happened today.
Snack Stop Vote: after every game, win or lose, the player picks the snack stop. No performance required.
DJ Rights: the player controls the music on the way home. Same rule after a win and after a loss.

items.title: What to Expect at Each Age and Division
items.summary: What tee ball, coach pitch, Minors, Majors, and the Intermediate and Junior divisions typically look like, and why your own league's pages are the final word.

video.note: Short clips from each division in order, tee ball through Juniors, with on-screen labels for typical ages, field size, who pitches, and the parent's role in each.

intro: Every league names and structures its divisions a little differently. One league's 'Minors' is another league's 'AA,' and age cutoffs shift from year to year. This guide describes what each level typically looks like so nothing surprises you, but your league's registration pages and its current Little League rulebook are the authority.
The pattern across all of them is the same: the field gets bigger, the pitching gets faster, and more of the real rules switch on. Each jump feels rough for the first two weeks. That is normal.
whatToDo: Find your league's own division page first and read it with your child. Ages, names, field sizes, and local rules are all there, and they beat anything written here.

Tee ball (typically ages 4 to 6, sometimes 7): the ball sits on a tee and every child bats each inning. Outs may be counted loosely or not at all, scores are often not kept, and games are short, usually an hour or less. The point is fun, basic throwing and catching, and learning which way to run. Expect dandelion picking in the outfield.

Coach pitch or machine pitch (typically ages 6 to 8): a coach or a pitching machine delivers slow, steady pitches so kids learn to hit a moving ball. Outs count, innings are real, and fielders start learning where to throw. Whether scores are kept depends on the league. GamePlanIQ's lesson on moving from tee ball to coach pitch is built for this jump.

Minors with kid pitchers (typically ages 8 to 11, sometimes split into levels): children pitch for the first time, so expect lots of walks, long innings, and big swings of emotion. Pitch count limits and rest days begin to matter here. Stealing and other baserunning rules vary widely by league at this level, so ask.

Majors (typically ages 10 to 12): the classic Little League you see on TV, usually with 60-foot base paths and the pitcher 46 feet from home plate. Full rules apply, players are often drafted onto teams, and the season may lead to All-Star selection. Runners typically may not leave the base until the pitch reaches the batter; check the rulebook for the exact wording.

Intermediate and Junior divisions (typically ages 11 to 14): the field grows (Intermediate often uses a 50-foot pitching distance and 70-foot bases; Juniors a full-size 60-foot and 90-foot field), and the game adds leading off, pickoffs, and more. The jump in field size is big; throws that used to be easy are suddenly long.
Expect your own role to change: in tee ball you may be on the field helping; by Majors you are in the bleachers. Ask the coach at the first meeting what parents do in this division.
Give any new division three weeks before worrying. Bigger field, faster pitches, new rules: the first two weeks are rough for everyone.
whatToSay: This year the field is bigger. Everyone's throws will be short for a while.
Coach pitch means the ball moves now. Watching it is the whole job.
Kids are pitching this year, so there will be lots of walks. That's normal.
What's one new rule you learned this season?
Let's look at the league's page together and see what your division does.
whatToWatchFor: Your child can tell you the big change in their division this year ('I have to wait for the pitch before I run').
By midseason, the new field size or pitch speed stops being the topic of every car ride.
If they pitch, they know the pitch count and rest rules apply to them, and they tell you when they pitched.
You know which rules in your division differ from TV baseball (leading off, stealing, dropped third strikes) because you looked them up.
whatToAvoid: Assuming your league's divisions match what a friend in another town described, or what this page describes. Names, ages, and rules vary; the league's pages win.
Pushing a child 'up' a division early for prestige. Playing with and against bigger, faster kids can shake confidence. Ask the coach for an honest read.
Expecting tee ball to look like baseball. If every child runs to the ball at once, the league is doing it right.
Counting walks and errors in Minors as 'bad baseball.' That is what learning to pitch and field looks like, every year, in every league.
Treating All-Stars as the point of the season. It is a small group for a few weeks; the season is the point.
ifStruggling: If your child is overwhelmed by a new division, ask the coach whether a different team or level is possible; many leagues allow a change early in the season.
Focus home practice on the one thing that changed: hitting a moving ball for new coach-pitch players, longer throws for a bigger field, watching the pitch for new leading-off rules.
Read the division's own rules page with your child; knowing the rules removes a lot of the fear.
Give it three weeks before making any decision about moving divisions.
makeItFun: Division Passport: a notebook page per division with the field size, the new rules, and one photo. Stamp it at the end of each season.
Field Walk: at the start of a new division, walk the new base distance together and count the steps. Then race it.
Rule Hunt: find three rules in the league's current rulebook that are different from last year's division and read them aloud like breaking news.
